briefs.argument: The can sits on the kitchen table for six seconds at 60% centrality — visible enough to read the script mark. While depiction alone is rarely actionable, the conservative path for E&O purposes is either a product-placement agreement (often free — Coca-Cola actively places product) or a two-second art-department swap to a greeked can.

precedents.holding: Deliberate set-dressing with protected material can be actionable where recognizable.
precedents.relevance: Cited by analogy for deliberate set-dressing, though trademark (not copyright) governs here.

briefs.argument: An ordinary soda can on a kitchen table is precisely the realistic incidental depiction courts protect in expressive works. There is no plot role, no disparagement, and no suggestion of sponsorship — under Rogers and Caterpillar, trademark owners cannot control truthful depictions of their products existing in the world. Productions depict branded consumer goods constantly without licenses.

precedents.holding: Trademark use in expressive works is protected absent artistic irrelevance or explicit misleading.
precedents.relevance: Incidental prop depiction has artistic relevance (realism) and implies no sponsorship.

precedents.case_name: Caterpillar Inc. v. Walt Disney Co.
precedents.holding: Depiction of branded products in film, without more, is not trademark infringement.
precedents.relevance: Directly on point for a background consumer product.

opinion.reasoning: Incidental background depiction of a consumer product in an expressive work is well protected (Rogers; Caterpillar) and Coca-Cola's enforcement posture toward film depiction is cooperative. Defensible as-is; a free placement agreement would convert the residual risk to zero if the producer prefers.
